```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 100)
library(peopleparser)

show <- function(x, cols = c("first_name", "middle_name", "last_name")) {
  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sanitize_input(x), parse_name))
  cbind(raw = x, out[cols])
}
```

Records list names in different orders: `JOHN A SMITH`, `SMITH JOHN A`,
`SMITH, JOHN`. Nothing in the string says which order was used, so
peopleparser guesses from how often each token is used as a given name or as
a surname. This article explains that evidence, the rules that use it for
names of two, three and more tokens, and the rules that keep compound
surnames (`VON KAMECKE`, `GARCIA LOPEZ`) together.

The rules run after cleaning, on the tokens that are left once titles,
credentials and suffixes are gone (see `vignette("name-cleaning")`).

## The evidence: first-name and surname counts

`census.names` counts how often each name is a first name and how often a
surname in U.S. Census Bureau name files (see `vignette("gender-scoring")` for
where the table comes from). `get_census_data()` looks up each token:

```{r}
get_census_data(c("JOHN", "SMITH", "JORDAN", "TAYLOR", "LESLIE", "KYUN"))
```

Some tokens are clearly one or the other (`JOHN`, `SMITH`). Others are both:
`JORDAN` and `TAYLOR` are common in both positions, and `LESLIE` is a common
surname too. `KYUN` is in neither list.

`check_if_surname()` turns the counts into a yes/no: a token reads as a
surname when more than half of its count is in the surname position. A token
found in neither list reads as a surname.

```{r}
x <- c("JOHN", "SMITH", "JORDAN", "TAYLOR", "LESLIE", "KYUN")
setNames(check_if_surname(x), x)
```

`determine_surname()` picks the single most likely surname in a name. It
ranks tokens by the share of their count in the surname position, with one
added to the surname count so that unknown tokens score high:

$$
p_{last} = \frac{1 + n_{last}}{1 + n_{first} + n_{last}}
$$

Ties go to the more common token, then to the later position.

```{r}
cd <- get_census_data(c("TAYLOR", "JORDAN"))
determine_surname(cd)   # position of the surname: JORDAN is first, TAYLOR the surname
```

## Rules by number of tokens

### One token

A lone token is treated as the surname.

```{r}
show(c("SMITH", "MADONNA"))
```

### Two tokens

The token that `determine_surname()` picks is the surname; the other is the
first name. Order in the string does not matter.

```{r}
show(c("JOHN SMITH", "SMITH JOHN", "JORDAN TAYLOR", "TAYLOR JORDAN",
       "LESLIE JAMES", "R BLINCOE"))
```

`LESLIE JAMES` shows the cost of this rule: both names are used in both
positions, and `JAMES` is the stronger given name, so the parse comes out as
`JAMES LESLIE`.

### Three tokens with one initial

A single-letter token is a middle initial (or a first initial). The rules
assume two orders, `FIRST M LAST` and `LAST FIRST M`:

* a trailing initial means the name was written surname first:
  `SMITH JOHN A` becomes `JOHN A SMITH`;
* an initial in the middle with a surname in front and a given name at the
  end (`SMITH J ALAN`) is also reordered;
* otherwise the order is kept.

```{r}
show(c("JOHN A SMITH", "SMITH JOHN A", "SMITH J ALAN", "J ALAN SMITH"))
```

The trailing-initial rule cannot tell `JOHN SMITH A` (given name first, stray
initial at the end) from `SMITH JOHN A`, and reads both as surname first.

### Three full tokens

`check_if_surname()` is applied to each token:

* surname, surname, given name (`GARCIA LOPEZ MARIA`): the given name moves to
  the front;
* surname, given name, any (`SMITH JOHN ALAN`): the first token moves to the
  end;
* otherwise the order is kept: first, middle, last.

```{r}
show(c("JOHN ALAN SMITH", "SMITH JOHN ALAN", "GARCIA LOPEZ MARIA"))
```

### Four or more tokens

The first token is the first name and `determine_surname()` picks the
surname. Everything else is the middle name. If the name opens with two
surnames followed by a given name (`SMITH JONES MARY ANN`), the two surnames
are joined into one.

```{r}
show(c("JOHN PAUL GEORGE RINGO", "SMITH JONES MARY ANN"))
```

## Compound surnames

Compound surnames are kept together by joining their parts with a dash, so
they stay one token through the rest of the parse. The census looks names up
with the dashes removed (`VON-KAMECKE` as `VONKAMECKE`).

### Surname particles

`prep_name()` and `fix_locative_surnames()` join a particle to the word after
it. The particles are `LA`, `VON`, `VAN`, `VANDER`, `DEL`, `DE`, `DI`, `DEN`,
`DER`, `MC` and `O`, plus `ST` inside a name (Saint) and `LO GRANDE`.

```{r}
fix_locative_surnames(c("Jane Van Dyke", "Mary von Diesel", "Dylan Van"))
show(c("THOMAS H VON KAMECKE", "SEAN ST CLAIR", "JULIA DI BUSSOLO"))
```

A particle at the end of a name (`Dylan Van`) has nothing to join and is
left alone. `ST` at the start of a name is not joined, because there it is
usually a title.

### Two surnames: middle tokens that read as surnames

After the first, middle and last names are assigned, a middle name of three or
more letters is checked again. If it reads as a surname, it is joined to the
last name:

* one middle token that reads as a surname joins the last name
  (`MARIA GARCIA LOPEZ` gives `GARCIA-LOPEZ`);
* with several middle tokens, an initial followed by a full token keeps the
  initial as the middle name and joins the rest to the surname;
* otherwise, everything from the first surname-like middle token on joins the
  surname, and the tokens before it stay as the middle name.

```{r}
show(c("MARIA GARCIA LOPEZ", "ELIZABETH ANNE WALKER SMITH",
       "JOHN Q PUBLIC SMITH"))
```

One exception: `MAY` is a common middle name and a surname. If it ends up at
the front of a compound surname, it is moved back to the middle name.

```{r}
show(c("SARAH MAY WILSON", "MARY MAY"))
```

### Titles that turned out to be names

When a token is both a title and a name (`EARL`, `MAJOR`), cleaning may strip
it and leave no first name. The parser then puts it back, using its position
in the original string: a leading token is the first name and a trailing one
is the surname. See `vignette("name-cleaning")`.

## Limits

* The rules know only how common each token is, not which order a source
  uses. If you know the source writes `LAST FIRST`, reorder the tokens before
  parsing.
* Tokens absent from the census read as surnames. A rare given name
  (`KYUN`) can end up as the surname. When both tokens read as surnames, the
  more common one wins: in `LUDWIG VAN BEETHOVEN`, `LUDWIG` (a census
  surname, never a census first name) beats the unlisted `VAN-BEETHOVEN`.
* A name that is both a common given name and a common surname (`JAMES`,
  `LESLIE`, `TAYLOR`, `JORDAN`) is decided by a small margin. Treat such
  parses as uncertain.
* A middle name that is also a surname (`ANNE WALKER`) is joined to the last
  name. That is right for Spanish and Portuguese double surnames and for
  maiden names kept as a middle name, but not for given middle names that are
  also surnames.
